content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus treats 'shadow' as a polyvalent biblical image with two competing primary senses: (1) divine protection and refuge (shadow of God's wings, Ps 91:1, Ps 17:8, Isa 25:4) and (2) typological foreshadowing — Old Testament law and institutions as a shadow of the substance found in Christ (Col 2:17; Heb 8:5; 10:1). All four responses also list, as common alternatives, the transience of human life (Job 8:9; Ps 144:4) and death/deep gloom ('the valley of the shadow of death,' Ps 23:4; Isa 9:2; Luke 1:79).","book_summary":"The book defines shadow as 'the covering of a greater presence' — a single unified sense embracing refuge under the Almighty's wings (Ps 91:1), a kingdom's protection over its people (Num 14:9, where the KJV renders the underlying word 'defence'), and the typological outline a coming body casts ahead of itself (Col 2:17). It insists the shadow is 'good to dwell in — not the gloom it is read as,' explicitly rejecting the darkness/gloom reading.","consensus_core_identification":"Shadow = a context-dependent image whose leading senses are (a) divine protection/refuge and (b) typological prefiguration of Christ, with transience and death/gloom as additional established senses.","book_core_identification":"Shadow = the covering cast by a greater presence — simultaneously protection (God/kingdom over people) and typological outline (the coming body of Christ) — a positive image, explicitly not gloom or darkness.","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book unifies the consensus's two rival primary senses (protection and typology) into one core identification ('covering of a greater presence'), so its core spans both dominant consensus readings. But it excludes cases the consensus admits: the death/gloom sense ('the shadow of death,' Ps 23:4, Isa 9:2, Luke 1:79) is expressly rejected ('not the gloom it is read as'), and the transience-of-life sense is silently dropped. It also adds cases such as Num 14:9, where a nation's protective 'shadow' is rendered 'defence,' extending the protective sense beyond God to a kingdom's covering.","material_contradiction":"No replacement of the central referent occurs; both leading consensus senses are preserved and fused. The disagreement is at the boundary: the book denies that gloom/darkness is a legitimate sense of shadow, whereas all four consensus responses treat it as a common, well-established meaning. This is exclusion of a peripheral sense, not contradiction of the core.","rationale":"The book's core identification retains and merges the consensus's two dominant senses — protection under God (matching Ps 91:1, the top verse in Responses A and B) and typological foreshadowing of Christ's body (matching Col 2:17, primary in Responses C and D). That is not mere restatement, however: the book (1) claims these are one meaning rather than parallel context-dependent senses, (2) explicitly rejects the gloom/death reading that every consensus response lists as common, and (3) drops the transience sense. This materially changes the extension while preserving the general referent/category, which is the definition of REFINED. It is not DIVERGENT because the central identification (protective/prefigurative covering) remains intact, and not MATCH because the boundary disagreement over gloom and the unification claim are real and material.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for MATCH: the consensus itself was split between protection and typology as primary, and the book simply affirms both; the rejection of gloom could be read as a lexical clarification (tsel vs. tsalmavet) rather than a substantive boundary change, since the consensus responses themselves note the death sense derives from a distinct Hebrew term. If the gloom exclusion is treated as a technical distinction the consensus would accept, the entry reduces to a wording-level restatement of consensus senses.","confidence":"high"}
